explanation: C++ supports both compile-time and runtime polymorphism.  Compile-time polymorphism, achieved through function overloading and templates, resolves function calls at compile time.  Runtime polymorphism, achieved through virtual functions and inheritance, resolves function calls at runtime based on the object's dynamic type. Understanding the difference is crucial for writing efficient and correct code.  Choosing the wrong type of polymorphism can lead to unexpected behavior or performance issues.
example_explanation: The example demonstrates runtime polymorphism.  The `area()` function is virtual, allowing the correct version (Circle or Square) to be called at runtime, even though the objects are accessed through a `Shape*` pointer.  This is crucial for flexible and extensible code. Compile-time polymorphism would require separate functions for each shape, making the code less maintainable and harder to extend to new shapes.  The explicit cleanup at the end shows best practice for preventing memory leaks when using dynamically allocated objects.  Ignoring this leads to resource exhaustion, a common pitfall in C++.
